newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda court sentences genocide leader to death. [CORRECTED 10:38 GMT 15/2]
newsitem.headline: Rwanda court sentences genocide leader to death. [CORRECTED 10:38 GMT 15/2]

text.p: A Kigali court on Friday sentenced a prominent former Rwandan politician to death for being a ringleader of the 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis despite being a Tutsi himself.
"He has war crimes on his head. He was leading the Interahamwe, guiding them here and killing even his own neighbours," said Presiding Judge Jariel Rutaremaram, sentencing Froduald Karamira to death.
Karamira, wearing a pink Rwandan convicts uniform, was grim-faced during sentencing in Nyamirambo commune. Onlookers jeered him as he was led out and his defence lawyer said he would appeal.

Karamira was a vice-president of the extremist MDR-Power party under the ousted Hutu-led government and is the most senior suspect found guilty in Rwanda of taking part in the mass slaughter of some 800,000 people.

He was accused of being a leader of the Interahamwe militia which led attacks in the capital Kigali and being responsible for inciting genocide through broadcasts on state-run Radio Rwanda and Radio Mille Collines (RTLM) during the bloodletting.

Karamira was born a Tutsi but using a Rwandan custom he converted to become a Hutu, the majority which ruled Rwanda until Tutsi rebels ousted them and put an end to the three-month genocide in July 1994.

The court also ordered him to pay 1.137 billion Rwandan francs ($3.8 million (corrects from $380,000)) in compensation to the families of his victims. State Rwanda radio described him as "one of the notorious planners of the 1994 genocide.
"We have to study the verdict. But for the moment, he wants to appeal," said his defence lawyer, Jose Luis de Cordoba of the agency Advocats sans Frontieres (Lawyers Without Borders).
Tutsi onlookers said they were not surprised by the death sentence. "The sentence was too light," said Patrick Buysa.
Karamira was arrested at Addis Ababa airport in Ethiopia last June and extradicted to Rwanda. He said during his trial he had no confidence in the courts ability to dispense justice.
At least 11 other Rwandans have been sentenced to death since Rwanda in December started trials of some of the 90,000 Hutu genocide suspects crammed into its prisons and lock-ups.
The international human rights group Amnesty International has expressed concern at the conduct of Rwandas genocide trials. Some accused have been sentenced to death without having a defence lawyer.
The United Nations has an international criminal tribunal for the Rwandan genocide with a maximum penalty of life imprisonment. It has 11 suspects detained at its Tanzania headquarters.
The tribunal said on Thursday four prominent Rwandans, including former colonel Theoneste Bagosora, accused of genocide will appear in court for the first time on February 19 and 20.
Bagosora was widely regarded as the most wanted suspect until he was extradited from Cameroon to Arusha on January 23.
A U.N. report this week said the tribunal was riddled with mismanagement, waste, unqualified personnel and bureaucratic infighting and not a single administrative area functioned effectively.
